Curvature, two boundary points and lattice counts

The Fourier transform of a curved surface receives its leading contributions where the frequency is normal to the surface. For a smooth convex body of positive curvature, there are exactly two such boundary points in each direction. Their phases and curvature factors yield a decay estimate. After smoothing the indicator, that estimate controls the error in counting lattice points in large dilates.

We use Surface transforms use the same kernel and Euclidean surface measure. All constants below are independent of the unit frequency direction.

Choose an orthonormal tangent basis by the finite Gram procedure. The resulting change of basis changes by a real congruence into the matrix of . Congruence preserves the positive and negative indices: maximal dimensions of subspaces on which a form is strictly positive or strictly negative are unchanged by an invertible map. Diagonalization identifies those dimensions with the numbers of positive and negative eigenvalues. This proves the signature assertion.

Proof: local stationary points. In a chart the amplitude is By Lemma 1, a normal point is a nondegenerate critical point, and the inverse normal map follows it smoothly as varies near its given direction. The earlier real stationary theorem applies on a sufficiently small fixed chart. Its leading factor is The ratio in this expression equals , by (C5).

Take its expansion at an integer depth . Every retained term of index is , since its coefficient is uniformly bounded on the smaller compact parameter patch. The remainder has that bound too. Thus the local leading expansion has the asserted absolute error. This argument uses the actual remainder of the earlier theorem.

Proof: compactness gives a uniform sum. Write . The normal incidence set is compact. To see closedness, work in any chart about a limit point and pass to the limit in . Every fiber over is discrete by the inverse normal map. It is a closed subset of compact , so it is finite: an infinite such subset would have an accumulation point in , contradicting local injectivity of either choice of normal.

Cover by finitely many smaller product neighborhoods where the local stationary argument just given applies. Complete these to a finite cover of by adding coordinate neighborhoods away from , and choose a smooth partition on a neighborhood of this compact set. Compact chart cutoffs from the earlier partition construction give this partition after dividing by their positive sum. Each stationary piece has its critical branch on a common parameter neighborhood; its amplitude can be extended by zero where that branch meets no support.

For each remaining piece the coordinate gradient of has a positive lower bound. Indeed it is nonzero on a compact set. The operator integrates by parts without boundary terms. Every derivative of its coefficients is on that piece; the product rule gives after iterations, uniformly in direction. There are finitely many pieces, so choose .

Sum their expansions. At each normal point the partition weights add to one. This gives exactly (C8), even where individual cutoffs vanish. Taking the maximum of finitely many constants proves uniformity on the full unit sphere.

The phase sign in (C8) can also be read from centers of curvature. With our convention , a principal eigenvalue has signed center displacement . Thus counts centers toward minus centers toward . This explains the sign when the opposite center-count convention is used.

In dimension , a smooth hypersurface is locally discrete. Its compactly supported density has finite support, and surface measure is counting measure. The empty curvature determinant is one and the empty Hessian has signature zero. The transform is exactly , so the corresponding zero-dimensional form of (C8) has zero remainder.

A convex boundary has exactly two relevant points

Let be a bounded nonempty open convex subset of with smooth boundary. Suppose the outward normal derivative has nonzero determinant everywhere on . For a convex set this condition is equivalent to positive principal curvatures with our convention, as the next proof shows. Write once positivity has been established.

Lemma 3. For every unit , there is exactly one boundary point with outward normal , and exactly one with outward normal . They depend smoothly on . At these points the Hessian signatures in (C8) are and , respectively. The curvatures have a positive lower bound on the whole boundary.

Here is the segment fact used in that argument. If , and , convexity gives balls of radius about for any tending to . Every point strictly within the limiting ball belongs to one of those balls for large . Thus . The supporting inequality extends from to by continuity.

Consequently the local graph satisfies , so is nonpositive. Formula (C6) gives in these orthonormal tangent coordinates. It is nonnegative and nonsingular, hence positive definite by real diagonalization. The same holds at every boundary point.

Proof: existence and uniqueness. The linear functional has a maximum and a minimum on compact . Neither extremum is interior, since a small movement in the direction remains in at any interior point. At a maximum the tangent derivatives vanish, and the supporting side determines the outward normal as ; at a minimum it is .

Two distinct maximizers would have their entire joining segment in and in the same supporting plane. This segment lies in , since an interior point cannot maximize a nonconstant linear functional. At an interior point of the segment, take its nonzero constant tangent velocity . Differentiating along the segment gives contradicting positive definiteness. The minimum is unique by the same argument. Conversely any point with outward normal maximizes that functional by the supporting inequality already proved. Hence these are the only two normal points.
